title: Why yawns are catching
hook: Seeing, hearing or even reading about a yawn can be enough to start one.
peek: Yawns spread from person to person, and you do not even need to see one. Hearing a yawn, or reading about yawning, works too. Some studies find people catch yawns most easily from family and close friends.
lede: Yawning is one of the most catching things people do. Watch someone yawn and there is a good chance you will follow within a few minutes. The psychologist Robert Provine spent years studying it and found the trigger can be surprisingly faint: a sound, a picture, or simply reading the word. Some readers will have yawned already.

bullets.text: Provine, at the University of Maryland, showed people films of a man yawning over and over. Around half of the viewers yawned while watching, far more than those shown a man smiling.
A common idea says yawns top up oxygen. Provine tested it in the 1980s by having people breathe air with extra oxygen or extra carbon dioxide. Their yawning did not change.

In 2011 Italian researchers Ivan Norscia and Elisabetta Palagi watched yawns spread in everyday life. They spread fastest between relatives, then friends, then acquaintances, and least between strangers. Some read this as a sign of empathy, but later studies have been mixed.
Young children rarely catch yawns. Studies suggest it becomes common around the age of four or five, though researchers disagree about why.
Why we yawn at all is still debated. One idea, from psychologist Andrew Gallup, is that a deep yawn helps cool the brain, but it remains a hypothesis rather than a settled answer.
